The Hawaiian crow, Corvus hawaiiensis, exhibits life-history traits shaped by its isolated island evolution. Neonates emerge from eggs with a wet weight at birth of approximately 14 grams [Wwb = approximately 14 grams], a modest mass that reflects the altricial state of newborn corvids. This initial size is followed by a period of rapid somatic development, leading to an ultimate wet weight for adults of about 520 grams [Wwi = about 520 grams], a value consistent with the species' position as a medium-sized member of its genus. In controlled captive rearing conditions maintained at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the age at birth, defined as the incubation period from laying to hatching, is 20 days [ab = 20 days]. This duration is typical for a crow of this body mass and aligns with developmental rates observed in other tropical corvids. The relatively short incubation stage contrasts sharply with the extended juvenile dependency that follows, a pattern common among large-brained passerines where parental investment must be sustained over many months.

Under the thermal conditions that characterize active metabolic periods in this species, specifically at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], several key developmental milestones have been documented for Hawaiian crow in managed care. The time since birth at fledging, marking the age when young birds first achieve sustained flight and leave the nest cavity, is 40 days after hatching [tx = 40 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Following this, the time since birth at puberty, denoting the onset of gonadal maturation and reproductive capability, occurs at 120 days after hatching [tp = 120 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. A considerable lag then separates this physiological readiness from actual breeding effort; the time since birth at first brood is recorded at 730 days after hatching [tR = 730 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This two-year delay before first successful reproduction reflects the complex social learning and territory acquisition required by this cooperatively breeding species, which necessitates a lengthy period as a non-breeding helper within family groups before an individual can secure its own nesting site.

Data on reproductive output for the Hawaiian crow provide further insight into its slow life-history pace. In a typical breeding season, females lay a single clutch of one to four eggs, with a modal clutch size of three eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = three eggs per nesting attempt]. The frequency of these reproductive events is constrained by the monsoonal climate, with most pairs producing only one successful brood each year [F_R_i = one successful brood each year]. This combination of modest clutch size and low annual fecundity yields a relatively low maximum reproductive rate for the species. When considered in the context of the entire adult lifespan, this annual output is consistent with the life-history strategy of a long-lived bird that invests heavily in the survival of each offspring through extended biparental and cooperative care. The limitation on reproductive events is further exacerbated by high rates of nest predation by the introduced small Indian mongoose, which has pushed many remaining wild pairs to breed in inaccessible cliffside cavities or, increasingly, within secure predator-proof aviaries.

Longevity records for this species, while primarily derived from captive populations, suggest a remarkable potential lifespan. The maximum documented lifespan for the Hawaiian crow under optimal managed care with veterinary oversight reaches approximately 27 years [am = approximately 27 years] at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], an exceptional duration for a passerine of this body size. Field records, however, suggest that wild `alalā face considerably higher mortality rates due to predation by the Hawaiian hawk, the `io, as well as from starvation during periods of drought when their primary food sources — native fruits and insects — become scarce. The stark contrast between captive and wild survivorship underscores the profound ecological pressure that has driven this species to functional extinction in its native habitat. A single free-flying individual recorded in the early 2000s was estimated to be at least 18 years of age based on annual resighting data, providing a rare glimpse of true wild longevity.

The physiological demands of maintaining a high core body temperature feature prominently in the daily energy budget of the Hawaiian crow. During periods of active foraging, when body temperature is regulated at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the birds exhibit elevated metabolic costs that must be met through continuous food intake. This high operating temperature is coupled with a relatively low maximal reproductive rate, formalized as a maximum of three offspring produced over the entire span of a single year [Ri = three offspring produced over the entire span of a single year], reflecting the species' inability to rapidly replace lost individuals. The 520-gram asymptotic adult body mass (520 grams) [Wwi = 520 grams] of the Hawaiian crow imposes a daily food intake requirement that renders the species acutely vulnerable to the loss of native fruiting trees — even minor reductions in habitat quality, such as the decline of the native `ōhi`a lehua tree whose fruits form a dietary staple, can have outsized impacts on body condition and consequently on nesting success. Future reintroduction efforts must therefore prioritize the restoration of diverse, fruit-rich forest understory to ensure that released birds can sustain the thermal and energetic requirements of a free-living existence.
